This page describes all the public classes, functions and modules of the `mcpl` Python package, as given by its built-in documentation (e.g. `help(mcpl.MCPLFile)`). Everything is available directly after `import mcpl`, except the contents of the `mcpl.plotting` and `mcpl.constants` modules.

## Reading files

### mcpl.MCPLFile (class)

```python
class MCPLFile(
    filename, blocklength=10000,
    raw_strings=False, select=None, edit=None)
```

Python-only class for reading MCPL files, using numpy and internal caches to ensure good efficiency. File access is read-only, and the particles can only be read in consecutive and forward order, providing either single particles or blocks of particles as requested.

Properties:

* `blocklength`: Number of particles read by each call to read\_block()
* `select`: Selection (ParticleFilter) applied when reading (None if no selection)
* `edit`: Edit (ParticleEdit) applied when reading (None if no edits)
* `version`: MCPL format version of the file
* `nparticles`: Number of particles in file
* `particlesize`: Uncompressed per-particle storage size in file \[bytes\]
* `headersize`: Uncompressed size of the file header \[bytes\]
* `endianness`: Endianness of numbers in file
* `opt_userflags`: Whether or not userflags are enabled in file
* `opt_universalpdgcode`: Global PDG code for all particles in file (a value of 0 means that PDG codes are stored per-particle)
* `opt_polarisation`: Whether or not polarisation info is enabled in file
* `opt_singleprec`: Whether or not floating point numbers in particle data are stored in single-precision (32bit) rather than double-precision (64bit)
* `opt_universalweight`: Global weight for all particles in file (a value of 0.0 means that weights are stored per-particle)
* `sourcename`: Name of application that wrote the MCPL file
* `comments`: List of custom comments (strings) embedded in the file header
* `blobs`: Dictionary of custom binary blobs (byte-arrays) embedded in the file header. Each such blob is associated with a key, which is also the key in the dictionary
* `blob_storage_order`: In-file storage order of binary blobs (as list of keys).
* `stat_sum`: Access `stat:sum:...` data from file comments as a convenient key-\>value dictionary. Note that any key present with a value of -1 in the file will get the value None here in the Python interface.

#### MCPLFile.read_block

```python
read_block()
```

Read and return next block of particles (None when EOF). Similar to read(), but returned `particle` object actually represents a whole block of particles, and the fields on it are thus (numpy) arrays of numbers rather than single numbers.  See also the particle\_blocks property for an iterator-based access to blocks.

#### MCPLFile.read

```python
read()
```

Read and return next particle in file (None when EOF) as a particle object, with particle state information available on fields as seen in the following example:

```python
p = mcplfile.read()
if p is not None:
     print(p.x,p.y,p.z)
     print(p.ux,p.uy,p.uz)
     print(p.polx,p.poly,p.polz)
     print(p.ekin,p.time,p.weight,p.userflags)
```

See also the particles property for an iterator-based access to particles. Furthermore, note that the read\_blocks() function and the particle\_blocks property provides block-based access, which can improve performance dramatically.

#### MCPLFile.skip_forward

```python
skip_forward(n)
```

skip n positions forward in file. (returns False when there is no

```python
particle at the new position, otherwise True)
```

#### MCPLFile.particles (property)

Use to iterate over all particles in file:

```python
for p in thefile.particles:
    print(p.x,p.y,p.z)
```

#### MCPLFile.particle_blocks (property)

Use to iterate over all particles in file, returning a block of particles each time for efficiency:

```python
for p in thefile.particle_blocks:
    #(NB: the "values" here are actually arrays)
    print(p.x,p.y,p.z)
```

#### MCPLFile.rewind

```python
rewind()
```

Rewind file, causing next calls to read() and read\_blocks() to start again at the beginning of the file.

#### MCPLFile.dump_hdr

```python
dump_hdr()
```

Dump file header to stdout (using a format identical to the one from the compiled mcpltool)

#### MCPLFile.dump_particles

```python
dump_particles(limit=10, skip=0, select=None)
```

Dump a list of particles to stdout (using a format identical to the one from the compiled mcpltool). The limit and skip parameters can be used to respectively limit the number of particles printed and to skip past particles at the head of the file. Use limit=0 to disable the limit. If select is given (an expression or a ParticleFilter), only the selected particles are shown, and limit and skip apply to those.

### mcpl.MCPLParticle (class)

```python
class MCPLParticle(block, idx)
```

Object representing a single particle

Properties:

* `position`: position as 3-dimensional array \[cm\]
* `direction`: normalised momentum direction as 3-dimensional array
* `polarisation`: polarisation vector as 3-dimensional array
* `x`: x-coordinate of position \[cm\]
* `y`: y-coordinate of position \[cm\]
* `z`: z-coordinate of position \[cm\]
* `ux`: x-coordinate of normalised momentum direction
* `uy`: y-coordinate of normalised momentum direction
* `uz`: z-coordinate of normalised momentum direction
* `polx`: x-coordinate of polarisation vector
* `poly`: y-coordinate of polarisation vector
* `polz`: z-coordinate of polarisation vector
* `ekin`: kinetic energy \[MeV\]
* `time`: time-stamp \[millisecond\]
* `weight`: weight or intensity
* `userflags`: custom per-particle flags
* `wavelength`: wavelength \[Aa\] (only for neutrons and gammas with non-zero kinetic energy, otherwise MCPLError is raised)
* `pdgcode`: MC particle number from the Particle Data Group (2112=neutron, 22=gamma, ...)
* `file_index`: Particle position in file (counting from 0)

### mcpl.MCPLParticleBlock (class)

```python
class MCPLParticleBlock(
    opt_polarisation, opt_userflags, opt_globalw,
    opt_globalpdg, fmtversion)
```

Object representing a block of particle. Fields are arrays rather than single numbers, but otherwise have the same meaning as on the MCPLParticle class.

Properties:

* `wavelength`: wavelength \[Aa\] (only for blocks with just neutrons and gammas, with non-zero kinetic energy, otherwise MCPLError is raised)
* `file_offset`: Particle position in file of first particle in block (counting from 0)
* `file_indices`: Array with the positions in the file of the particles in the block (counting from 0), also for blocks with selected particles.
* `polx`: X-coordinate of polarisation vector of each particle (array)
* `poly`: Y-coordinate of polarisation vector of each particle (array)
* `polz`: Z-coordinate of polarisation vector of each particle (array)
* `pdgcode`: MC particle number from the Particle Data Group (2112=neutron, 22=gamma, ...) of each particle (array)
* `weight`: Weight or intensity of each particle (array)
* `userflags`: Custom per-particle flags of each particle (array)
* `position`: Positions \[cm\] as array with shape (N,3)
* `polarisation`: Polarisation vectors as array with shape (N,3)
* `direction`: Normalised momentum directions as array with shape (N,3)
* `x`: X-coordinate of position \[cm\] of each particle (array)
* `y`: Y-coordinate of position \[cm\] of each particle (array)
* `z`: Z-coordinate of position \[cm\] of each particle (array)
* `time`: Time-stamp \[millisecond\] of each particle (array)
* `ux`: X-coordinate of normalised momentum direction of each particle (array)
* `uy`: Y-coordinate of normalised momentum direction of each particle (array)
* `uz`: Z-coordinate of normalised momentum direction of each particle (array)
* `ekin`: Kinetic energy \[MeV\] of each particle (array)

## Writing files

### mcpl.MCPLOutFile (class)

```python
class MCPLOutFile(
    filename, *, sourcename=None, comments=None,
    blobs=None, stat_sum=None,
    opt_userflags=False, opt_polarisation=False,
    opt_singleprec=True, opt_universalpdgcode=0,
    opt_universalweight=0.0, blocklength=10000,
    select=None, edit=None)
```

Python-only class for writing MCPL files, using numpy to process blocks of particles efficiently. The produced files are identical to those written by the C library (MCPL format version 3).

The header is configured with methods named like the corresponding functions in the C API (hdr\_set\_srcname, hdr\_add\_comment, hdr\_add\_data, hdr\_add\_stat\_sum, enable\_userflags, enable\_polarisation, enable\_doubleprec, enable\_universal\_pdgcode, enable\_universal\_weight), and/or by passing keyword arguments to the constructor, named like the corresponding attributes of MCPLFile (sourcename, comments, blobs, stat\_sum, opt\_userflags, opt\_polarisation, opt\_singleprec, opt\_universalpdgcode, opt\_universalweight). The two can be mixed freely, since the keyword arguments are simply passed on to the methods. As in the C API, the header must be completely configured before the first particle is added, except for stat:sum values which can be updated until the file is closed (if a value was registered before the first particle, for instance the special value -1).

Particles are added in blocks with add\_particles(..), or one at a time with add\_particle(..). The file must be closed with close() or closeandgzip(), which happens automatically (with close()) at the end of a with-statement:

```python
with MCPLOutFile('myfile.mcpl',
                 sourcename='MySimulation',
                 opt_universalpdgcode=2112) as f:
    f.hdr_add_comment('Some comment')
    f.add_particles( position = pos,
                     direction = dirs,
                     ekin = ekin, time = t,
                     weight = w )
```

Particles read from an existing file with MCPLFile (blocks or single particles) can be passed directly to add\_particles(..) and add\_particle(..), in which case the packed particle data is transferred exactly when possible (like mcpl\_transfer\_last\_read\_particle in the C API). The header settings of an existing file can be copied with transfer\_metadata(..).

Properties:

* `filename`: Name of file being written to (might have had .mcpl appended)
* `nparticles`: Number of particles added so far
* `sourcename`: Name of the generating application (None if not set). Like the other header properties, it is decoded like by MCPLFile.
* `comments`: List of comments added so far (strings)
* `blobs`: Dictionary of binary blobs added so far (with strings as keys)
* `stat_sum`: Dictionary of stat:sum entries, like MCPLFile.stat\_sum
* `opt_userflags`: Whether userflags are stored for each particle
* `opt_polarisation`: Whether polarisation vectors are stored for each particle
* `opt_singleprec`: Whether floating point numbers are stored in single precision (rather than double precision)
* `opt_universalpdgcode`: Universal pdgcode (0 if not set)
* `opt_universalweight`: Universal weight (0.0 if not set)
* `particlesize`: Bytes per particle in the file

#### MCPLOutFile.hdr_add_stat_sum

```python
hdr_add_stat_sum(key, value)
```

Add or update named statistics `sum`, encoded in a special comment (see the C API for details). Use value=-1 (or None) to register a value which will be updated later (at the latest before closing the file).

#### MCPLOutFile.hdr_scale_stat_sums

```python
hdr_scale_stat_sums(scale)
```

Scale all stat:sum values with a given factor which must be a finite number \>0.0 or -1 (see the C API for details).

#### MCPLOutFile.transfer_metadata

```python
transfer_metadata(source)
```

Transfer all settings, blobs and comments from an MCPLFile object (or the file with the given name). Note that if splitting files rather than filtering them, hdr\_scale\_stat\_sums should be called afterwards (see the C API for details).

#### MCPLOutFile.add_particles

```python
add_particles(particles=None, **fields)
```

Add block of particles. Particle data is specified with keyword arguments using the field names of MCPLParticleBlock: position (as array with shape (N,3)) or x, y, z; direction or ux, uy, uz; polarisation or polx, poly, polz; ekin, time, weight, pdgcode, userflags. Values can be numpy arrays of length N or scalars (which apply to all particles), and missing fields default to 0. Like in the C API, fields not enabled in the file are ignored (e.g. polarisation unless enable\_polarisation() was called) as are the weight and pdgcode fields in files with universal weight or pdgcode.

Instead of ekin, the wavelength \[Aa\] can be specified for neutrons and gammas.

Alternatively, an MCPLParticleBlock (or an MCPLParticle) read with MCPLFile can be passed, in which case its packed data is transferred exactly whenever possible. Combined with keyword arguments, the given fields replace those of the passed particles (e.g. to edit positions or weights), for instance: f.add\_particles( block, weight = 2 \* block.weight ).

#### MCPLOutFile.add_particle

```python
add_particle(particle=None, **fields)
```

Add single particle. Takes the same arguments as add\_particles(..), but with scalar values (or vectors of length 3), or a single MCPLParticle read with MCPLFile. Particles are internally buffered and written in blocks for efficiency.

#### MCPLOutFile.close

```python
close()
```

Close the file (writing all pending particles and updating the header).

#### MCPLOutFile.closeandgzip

```python
closeandgzip()
```

Close the file and gzip it (which will append .gz to the filename). Returns True if gzipping was successful.

### mcpl.gzip_file

```python
gzip_file(filename)
```

Compress file with gzip, replacing it with a file with .gz appended to its name (like mcpl\_gzip\_file in the C API). Returns True if successful.

## File operations

### mcpl.can_merge

```python
can_merge(file1, file2)
```

Check if two MCPL files can be merged (like mcpl\_can\_merge in the C API). This requires everything in the headers except the number of particles and the values of stat:sum entries to be identical.

### mcpl.convert2ascii

```python
convert2ascii(mcplfile, outfile)
```

Read particle contents of mcplfile and write into outfile using a simple ASCII-based format

### mcpl.create_outfile_mpi

```python
create_outfile_mpi(
    filename, iproc, nproc, **kwargs)
```

Create output file for worker process iproc out of nproc (like mcpl\_create\_outfile\_mpi in the C API). The worker files must be closed with closeandgzip(), after which merge\_outfiles\_mpi can be used to merge them into the final file. Keyword arguments are passed on to MCPLOutFile.

### mcpl.dump_file

```python
dump_file(
    filename, header=True, particles=True,
    limit=10, skip=0, select=None, **kwargs)
```

Python equivalent of mcpl\_dump(..) function from mcpl.h, which can be used to dump both header and particle contents of a file to stdout. If select is given (an expression or a ParticleFilter), only the selected particles are shown.

### mcpl.forcemerge_files

```python
forcemerge_files(
    file_output, files, keep_userflags=False)
```

Merge particle contents of a list of files, even if they are not compatible, at the price of discarding most meta-data like comments and blobs (like mcpl\_forcemerge\_files in the C API). Userflags are discarded unless keep\_userflags is set. Returns the new file as an open MCPLOutFile object, which must be closed with close() or closeandgzip().

### mcpl.merge_files

```python
merge_files(file_output, files)
```

Merge the particle contents of a list of compatible files into a new file (like mcpl\_merge\_files in the C API). Values of stat:sum entries are added up. Returns the new file as an open MCPLOutFile object, which must be closed with close() or closeandgzip().

### mcpl.merge_inplace

```python
merge_inplace(file1, file2)
```

Append the particle contents of file2 to file1 (like mcpl\_merge\_inplace in the C API). The files must be compatible, and file1 must not be gzipped. Values of stat:sum entries are added up.

### mcpl.merge_outfiles_mpi

```python
merge_outfiles_mpi(filename, nproc)
```

Merge the gzipped worker files created with create\_outfile\_mpi into the final gzipped output file and remove them (like mcpl\_merge\_outfiles\_mpi in the C API).

### mcpl.name_helper

```python
name_helper(filename, mode)
```

Estimate the output name of a given filename (like mcpl\_name\_helper in the C API), which can be relative or absolute and with or without .mcpl or .mcpl.gz suffixes. The mode controls the returned name: `M` for /abs/path/base.mcpl, `G` for /abs/path/base.mcpl.gz, `B` for /abs/path/base, and `m`, `g`, `b` for the same without the directory.

### mcpl.repair

```python
repair(filename)
```

Repair a file which was not properly closed, or which was truncated, by updating the number of particles in the header and removing any incomplete particle data at the end (like mcpl\_repair in the C API).

## Expressions

### mcpl.ParticleEdit (class)

```python
class ParticleEdit(expression)
```

Modification of particle fields given by an expression with statements separated by commas, which are evaluated with numpy on blocks of particles. For instance:

```python
edit = ParticleEdit("rotate_z(90deg), z += 10cm,"
                    " wavelength = 1.8Aa")
for block in mcplfile.particle_blocks:
    outfile.add_particles( block, **edit(block) )
```

The statements are executed in order, so each statement sees the results of the previous ones. The statements are:

* Assignments to fields, like `x = 2m*ux` or `z += 1cm` (also -=, \*=, and /=), where the right hand sides use the syntax of ParticleFilter. The values must have the units of the field (e.g. a length for x). Assigning wavelength changes the kinetic energy of neutrons and gammas.
* Assignments to variables (lowercase names which are not names of fields, units, constants or functions), which can be used in later statements, for instance to keep original values: `tmp = x, x = y, y = tmp`. Variables keep the units of their values.
* swap(a,b), which exchanges the values of two fields (or variables) with the same units, e.g. `swap(x,y)`.
* rotate\_x(angle), rotate\_y(angle), rotate\_z(angle), which rotate the position, direction and polarisation of the particles around the given axis (through the origin), e.g. `rotate_y(90deg)`. The rotation is counter-clockwise when looking from the positive axis towards the origin. Rotations by multiples of 90 degrees are exact (e.g. `rotate_z(90deg)` changes (x,y) to exactly (-y,x)), and rotations never give negative zeros (-0.0).

Properties:

* `expression`: The expression (with normalised whitespace)
* `modified_fields`: Names of the fields which the edit can modify (ekin for edits of the wavelength).

### mcpl.ParticleFilter (class)

```python
class ParticleFilter(expression)
```

Selection of particles based on an expression, which is evaluated with numpy on blocks of particles. For instance:

```python
flt = ParticleFilter("pdgcode == neutron"
                     " && ekin < 25meV"
                     " && abs(x) <= 2mm")
for block in mcplfile.particle_blocks:
    selected = block[ flt(block) ]
```

Whitespace (including newlines) is only used to separate the parts of expressions, so long expressions can be written over several lines. The expression syntax is like in C: particle fields (x, y, z, ux, uy, uz, polx, poly, polz, ekin, time, weight, pdgcode, userflags, and wavelength), numbers, arithmetic (+, -, \*, /, %, and ^ or \*\* for powers), comparisons (which can be chained, as in `0 < x < 2cm`), logical operations (&&, \|\|, ! or and, or, not), bitwise &, \| and ~ on integers (e.g. on userflags, as in `userflags & 0x10`, where like in C integers which are not 0 are true), functions (sqrt, abs, floor, ceil, exp, log, log10, sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, atan2, hypot, min, max), the constant pi, and the names neutron, antineutron, proton, antiproton, electron, positron (or antielectron), muon, antimuon, and gamma (or photon), which can be used for pdgcode values. The wavelength is only defined for neutrons and gammas, so it is an error to use it for other particles, and expressions must select neutrons or gammas before using it, as in `pdgcode == neutron && wavelength > 1.8Aa` (the right side of && is only evaluated for particles where the left side is true, and the right side of \|\| only for particles where the left side is false, like in C).

Values with units must always be given with units (except for a plain 0, as in `x > 0`): meV, eV, keV, MeV, GeV, TeV (energy), ns, us, ms, s (time), Aa, nm, um, mm, cm, m, km (length, also for wavelengths), as in `ekin < 25meV`, `wavelength > 0.18nm` or `x^2 + y^2 < 4cm^2`. The units deg and rad can be used for angles (which are otherwise in radians), as in `acos(uz) < 10deg`. Expressions with missing or inconsistent units, like `x < 2` or `x < 1meV`, are rejected.

Properties:

* `expression`: The expression (with normalised whitespace)

### mcpl.ParticleValue (class)

```python
class ParticleValue(expression)
```

Numerical value calculated from particle fields with an expression (with the syntax of ParticleFilter), for instance for histograms. The expression must not have units, so values with units must be divided by a unit, as in `ekin/MeV` or `hypot(x,y)/mm`. Boolean expressions (like `x > 0cm`) give 1 for true and 0 for false. For instance:

```python
val = ParticleValue("ekin/meV")
for block in mcplfile.particle_blocks:
    print( val(block) )
```

Properties:

* `expression`: The expression (with normalised whitespace)

## Statistics and histograms

### mcpl.Histogram (class)

```python
class Histogram(
    expression, edges, logx, weighted, lethargy,
    title)
```

1D histogram of the values of an expression, created by the histogram() function. The bin edges are in edges, and the contents (sums of weights, or numbers of particles if unweighted) in the dictionary contents, with one entry per curve (keyed by label, None for a single curve). The sums of squared weights are in sumw2 (with the same keys), and the sums of weights below and above the range of the edges are in underflow and overflow.

Properties:

* `ylabel`: Label of the values (e.g. `weights per bin`)

#### Histogram.values

```python
values(label=None)
```

Values to plot: the contents, or for lethargy plots the contents divided by the bin widths in lethargy (ln(E2/E1)).

#### Histogram.panel

```python

```

Panel (see mcpl.plotting) with the histogram.

```python

```

#### Histogram.plot


Show the histogram (or save it in a file if filename is given) with the plotting backend (name or Backend object, default is the default backend, see mcpl.plotting). Further keyword arguments are options for the backend (e.g. matplotlib\_backend='agg'). Returns the list of created files when saving.

### mcpl.collect_stats

```python
collect_stats(
    mcplfile, stats='all', bin_data=True,
    select=None)
```

Efficiently collect statistics from an entire file. Returns dictionary with stat names as key and the collected statistics as values. If select is given (an expression or a ParticleFilter), only the selected particles are included.

### mcpl.dump_stats

```python
dump_stats(stats)
```

Format and print provided statistics object to stdout. The stats object is assumed to have been created by a call to collect\_stats()

### mcpl.histogram

```python
histogram(
    files, expression, select=None, bins=100,
    range=None, logx=False, weighted=True,
    split=None, lethargy=False, max_curves=8)
```

Histogram of the values of an expression (see ParticleValue) for the particles in one or more files. Values with units must be divided by a unit, e.g. `ekin/MeV`. For instance:

```python
h = mcpl.histogram( "myfile.mcpl", "ekin/eV",
                    select = "pdgcode == neutron",
                    logx = True, lethargy = True )
h.plot()
```

Particles can be selected with the select expression (see ParticleFilter). The number of bins and their range (a tuple (low,high)) can be given, otherwise the range covers all values. With logx, the bins are logarithmic. Unless weighted is False, the histogram contains the sum of weights in each bin rather than the number of particles. With lethargy (which implies logx), the plotted values are divided by the bin widths in lethargy (ln(E2/E1)), as is common for energy spectra.

With split (an expression), there is a separate curve for each value of the expression (for at most max\_curves values, any others are combined into a curve labelled `other`), for instance split=`pdgcode` gives a curve for each particle type, and split=`x > 0cm` one for each half. With more than one file, there is a curve for each file.

### mcpl.histogram2d

```python
histogram2d(
    files, xexpression, yexpression, select=None,
    bins=100, xrange=None, yrange=None,
    weighted=True)
```

2D histogram of the values of two expressions (see histogram()) for the particles in one or more files, for instance:

```python
h = mcpl.histogram2d( "myfile.mcpl",
                      "x/cm", "y/cm" )
h.plot()
```

### mcpl.plot_histograms

```python
plot_histograms(
    histograms, filename=None, backend=None,
    logy=False, overlay=False, labels=None,
    **options)
```

Show histograms (or save them in a file if filename is given) with the plotting backend and options (see Histogram.plot). Each histogram is shown in a separate figure (e.g. on separate pages of a PDF file), or with overlay=True, all the (1D) histograms are drawn in the same plot with a legend, for instance to compare histograms of the same expression from different simulations. The legend shows the labels if given, and otherwise the titles (selections) or expressions of the histograms. Returns the list of created files when saving.

### mcpl.plot_stats

```python
plot_stats(
    stats, pdf=False, set_backend=None,
    backend=None, filename=None, **options)
```

Produce plots of provided statistics object (from collect\_stats(), or a file for which collect\_stats() is called). The plots are shown interactively, or saved in a file if filename is given, in the format given by its extension (e.g. `plots.pdf`, or `plots.png` which gives one numbered file per plot). The backend parameter selects the plotting backend (name or Backend object, default is the default backend, see mcpl.plotting), and further keyword arguments are options for it (e.g. matplotlib\_backend='agg'). Returns the list of created files when saving. The pdf and set\_backend parameters are deprecated (use filename and matplotlib\_backend instead).

### mcpl.stats_figures

```python
stats_figures(stats)
```

Figures (see mcpl.plotting) with plots of the statistics collected with collect\_stats() (or a file, for which collect\_stats() is called): an overview page, and a page for each field.

## Other

### mcpl.MCPLError (class)

```python
class MCPLError(...)
```

Common exception class for all exceptions raised by module

### mcpl.app_pymcpltool

```python
app_pymcpltool(argv=None)
```

Implements a python equivalent of the compiled MCPL tool. If no argv list is passed in, sys.argv will be used. In case of errors, MCPLError exceptions are raised. Messages are always printed, even if use\_logging() was called.

### mcpl.encode_stat_sum

```python
encode_stat_sum(key, value)
```

Function which can help encode a key and value into the special format needed for `stat:sum:...` comments in MCPL headers. A value of either None or -1.0 maps to -1.0 in the encoding.

### mcpl.is_valid_stat_sum_key

```python
is_valid_stat_sum_key(key)
```

Function which can be used to verify that a particular key has the correct format needed for `stat:sum:...` comments in MCPL headers.

### mcpl.use_logging

```python
use_logging(enable=True)
```

Send messages and warnings from MCPL to the logger named `mcpl` (as logging.INFO and logging.WARNING records), instead of printing them to stdout (prefixed with `MCPL:` and `MCPL WARNING:`), which is the default. After that, they are controlled by the logging configuration of the application, e.g.:

```python
import logging
import mcpl
mcpl.use_logging()
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
```

Calling use\_logging(False) switches back to printing. Note that this does not affect functions which are meant to print (like dump\_file), nor the pymcpltool command, which always prints.

## mcpl.plotting

Backend-independent description of plots, and functions to show or save them. Plots are described with the Figure, Panel and item classes below (which hold numbers, not graphics objects), and are drawn by one of the plotting backends: matplotlib or plotly (see available\_backends()), unicode or ascii (which draw the plots as text, in the terminal or in .txt files), or a custom backend (see Backend and register\_backend()).

Unless a backend is specified when plotting, the default backend is used: the one set with set\_default\_backend(), or else the one named by the MCPL\_PLOT\_BACKEND environment variable, or else the first available one.

For instance:

```python
from mcpl.plotting import Figure, Panel, StepHist
from mcpl.plotting import save
hist = StepHist(edges,values)
panel = Panel( title = 'My histogram',
               xlabel = 'x [cm]',
               items = [ hist ] )
save( Figure( panels = [ panel ] ), 'myplot.pdf' )
```

### mcpl.plotting.Backend (class)

```python
class Backend()
```

Interface of plotting backends (public as mcpl.plotting.Backend), which show or save lists of Figure objects. Subclasses set name (a unique name used to select the backend), formats (the file extensions which save() can create), and requirement (the Python package needed, if any), and implement show() and save(), and is\_available() if not always available. Options can be given as keyword arguments to \_\_init\_\_, named with the backend name as prefix (like matplotlib\_backend).

#### Backend.is_available

```python
is_available(cls)
```

Whether the backend can be used (e.g. if its requirement is installed). This should not import any heavy modules.

#### Backend.available_formats

```python
available_formats(cls)
```

File extensions which save() can create in this installation

#### Backend.show

```python
show(figures)
```

Show the figures interactively.

#### Backend.save

```python
save(figures, filename)
```

Save the figures in a file, with format given by the extension of the filename (one of the available formats). If the format can only hold a single figure, and there are more figures, files with numbered names are created (e.g. plot\_1.png, plot\_2.png). Returns the list of created files.

#### Backend.check_format

```python
check_format(filename)
```

Extension of filename, if it is an available format (otherwise MCPLError is raised).

```python
class Bars(labels, values, horizontal=False)
```

Bar chart with a bar for each label (horizontal if horizontal is set).

#### Figure.add

```python
class Panel(
```

One plot (a set of axes) with items like StepHist objects. Items with labels are shown in a legend.

#### Panel.add

### mcpl.plotting.StepHist (class)

```python
class StepHist(
    edges, values, label=None, color=None)
```

1D histogram drawn as a step line. The bin edges have one more entry than the values. The color is an index into the colour cycle of the backend (by default the position of the item in the panel).

### mcpl.plotting.Text (class)

```python
class Text(text)
```

Message shown in the middle of a panel (e.g. `No data`).

### mcpl.plotting.available_backends

```python
available_backends()
```

Names of the plotting backends which can be used (i.e. for which the required Python packages are installed), in order of preference.

### mcpl.plotting.formats

```python
formats(backend=None)
```

File extensions of the formats which the backend (name or Backend object, default is the default backend) can save in this installation.

### mcpl.plotting.register_backend

```python
register_backend(backend_class)
```

Register a custom plotting backend, a subclass of Backend, which can then be selected by its name (it is added after the built-in backends in the order of preference).

### mcpl.plotting.save

```python
save(figures, filename, backend=None, **options)
```

Save a Figure (or a list of figures) in a file, with the plotting backend of the given name (or a Backend object, default is the default backend). The format is given by the extension of the filename: .pdf, .png or .svg with matplotlib, .html with plotly (or .pdf, .png or .svg if the kaleido package is installed), and .txt with unicode and ascii. If the format can only hold one figure, and there are more figures, the files get numbered names (e.g. plot\_1.png, plot\_2.png). Returns the list of created files. Further keyword arguments are options for the backend (see show()).

### mcpl.plotting.set_default_backend

```python
set_default_backend(backend)
```

Set the plotting backend to use when no backend is specified: the name of a backend, or a Backend object. If that backend is not available when plotting, an error is raised. Use None to go back to using the MCPL\_PLOT\_BACKEND environment variable (if set) or the first available backend.

### mcpl.plotting.show

```python
show(figures, backend=None, **options)
```

Show a Figure (or a list of figures) interactively, with the plotting backend of the given name (or a Backend object, default is the default backend). Further keyword arguments are options for the backend, named with the backend name as prefix (e.g. matplotlib\_backend='qtagg' or plotly\_renderer='browser').

## mcpl.constants

Physical constants used by MCPL.

The values are the CODATA 2022 recommended values of the fundamental physical constants (released by NIST in May 2024, https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants/ ), where the Planck constant, the speed of light and the elementary charge are exact by the definition of the SI units (since 2019). The neutron mass is the only measured value used.

The constants are given in SI units, and the derived values in the units used by MCPL (MeV for energies, and Aa for wavelengths).

| Name | Value |
|---|---|
| `c_light` | `299792458.0` |
| `e_charge` | `1.602176634e-19` |
| `h_planck` | `6.62607015e-34` |
| `hc_eV_Aa` | `12398.419843320025` |
| `neutron_mass` | `1.67492750056e-27` |
| `neutron_mass_energy` | `939.5654219340053` |
